card.title: Merge a branch back
card.blurb: One command brings a branch home - and it does two different things. Run `git merge` when `main` stayed put, then again when it did not.
hero.eyebrow: Git · Part three · Bringing work back
hero.title: Merge a branch back
intro.0: Your branch works, and now it has to become part of `main`. That is the step people hesitate over - it feels like where things get broken. It is one command, and it behaves in two different ways. Which way you get depends on nothing you type: only on whether `main` moved while you were away. Here you run it both ways and watch the graph answer for you.
task.1.title: Bring back the branch that is ahead
task.1.context:
Two branches sit beside `main` here, `docs` and `fix`. Only one of them holds a commit `main` has not got.

`git log --oneline` lists what `main` can already reach, and names every branch sitting on those commits. A branch missing from that list is the one still holding something.
task.1.goal.0: Run `git branch` to see which branches exist.
task.1.goal.1: Run `git log --oneline` to see which of them `main` already contains.
task.1.goal.2: Standing on `main`, merge the one that is missing from the log.
task.1.goal.3: Nothing new is saved and two names end up on one commit - that is a fast-forward.
task.2.title: Bring it back when both sides moved
task.2.context:
Same two branches, and `main` has committed since the split.

One log is not enough now. Read what `main` holds, then stand on the branch that was missing from it and read that too. When each side holds a commit the other has never seen, sliding a name forward would leave one of them off the line.
task.2.goal.0: Read `git log --oneline` on `main`, then switch to the branch it does not contain and read its log too.
task.2.goal.1: Come back to `main` and merge that branch.
task.2.goal.2: A commit appears that neither branch had before.
task.2.goal.3: It has two parents - one line running back to each side.
task.3.title: Merge a branch back - recap
task.3.context: One command, two shapes - decided by where the names were sitting.
task.3.summaryIntro: Merging is not one fixed move. Git looks at whether the branch you are standing on has added anything since the split, and then picks the smallest thing that works. Which branch to name is your call, and the log is where you settle it.
task.3.summaryItems.0.title: Merge -
task.3.summaryItems.0.text: bringing another branch's commits into the one you are on, so two lines become one.
task.3.summaryItems.1.title: `git log --oneline` -
task.3.summaryItems.1.text: lists what your branch already reaches, and names the branches sitting on those commits.
task.3.summaryItems.2.title: Fast-forward -
task.3.summaryItems.2.text: what you get when your branch added nothing; git slides its name forward and saves no commit.
task.3.summaryItems.3.title: Merge commit -
task.3.summaryItems.3.text: what you get when both sides moved; it is the one commit with two parents.
task.3.summaryItems.4.title: `git merge fix` -
task.3.summaryItems.4.text: the same line either way, so read the graph to see which one you got.
task.3.summaryClose: Next: what happens when both sides changed the same file, and git stops to ask you.
